meta.blurb: Anne Elliot once let herself be persuaded to give up the man she loved. Eight years later, Captain Wentworth returns, rich, proud and still hurt. Jane Austen's gentlest love story asks whether a second chance can ever be as sweet as the first.
meta.bible: Sir Walter Elliot: a vain baronet of Kellynch Hall in Somerset; loves his looks and his rank; spends too much money. Elizabeth Elliot: his eldest daughter, handsome, cold and proud. Anne Elliot: his middle daughter, 27, gentle, wise and often overlooked; the heroine. Mary Musgrove: his youngest daughter, who is married and always complains of her health. Charles Musgrove: Mary's good-natured husband, who lives at Uppercross. Lady Russell: a wise older friend of the family and Anne's godmother figure; she persuaded Anne eight years ago. Mr Shepherd: Sir Walter's lawyer. Admiral Croft: a cheerful naval officer who rents Kellynch Hall. Mrs Croft: the Admiral's wife, Sophia, who is Captain Wentworth's sister. Frederick Wentworth: a naval officer; poor when Anne first loved him, now a rich and respected Captain. Mr and Mrs Musgrove: Charles's parents, kind and simple, of Uppercross Hall. Louisa Musgrove and Henrietta Musgrove: Charles's lively sisters. Charles Hayter: Henrietta's cousin and sweetheart, a young clergyman. Captain Harville: a naval officer living at Lyme, lame from a wound. Captain Benwick: a sad, bookish officer whose fiancee Fanny Harville has died. Mr William Elliot: Sir Walter's cousin and heir, charming but selfish. Mrs Clay: Mr Shepherd's daughter, a friend of Elizabeth who wants to marry Sir Walter. Mrs Smith: Anne's old school friend, now poor, ill and a widow in Bath. Places: Kellynch Hall; Somerset; Uppercross; Winthrop; Lyme; the Cobb, the long stone sea wall at Lyme; Bath; Camden Place; the Octagon Room, where the concert is held; the White Hart, an inn in Bath; Westgate Buildings. Time: 1814, just after the long war with France. Voice and tone: gentle, witty and tender; Anne's feelings are quiet and deep; the second chance is earned, never rushed.

B1B2: Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall was a vain man who admired his own face and his noble name. Every evening he opened the book of noble families and read the page about his own family.
Lady Elliot had died many years before, leaving Sir Walter with three daughters. Elizabeth was proud like her father, Mary was often unhappy, and gentle Anne was ignored by almost everyone at home.
Sir Walter loved fine clothes, grand dinners and handsome furniture, and he had spent far more than he earned. Lady Russell begged him to save money, but he could not bear to give up anything.

Mr Shepherd suggested that Sir Walter should rent out Kellynch Hall and live more cheaply in the city of Bath. The war with France was over, he said, and many rich naval officers were looking for a fine house.

Admiral Croft, a cheerful sailor, agreed to rent Kellynch Hall, and his wife came with him to see it. Anne learned that Mrs Croft was the sister of Frederick Wentworth, and the name made her heart beat faster.
When Anne was nineteen, she had met Frederick Wentworth, a young naval officer who was clever, brave and full of fire. They had fallen in love quickly, although he had no money and no family name.
Lady Russell thought the match was unwise, because he was poor and his future was uncertain. She spoke so kindly and so firmly that Anne gave way, and the engagement was broken.
Eight years had passed, and Anne had lost her youth and her pretty colour. She had never loved another man, and she had heard that Captain Wentworth had become rich and famous in the war.

Sir Walter and Elizabeth left for Bath with Mrs Clay, a friend who made herself very useful. Anne stayed behind to say goodbye to the house, and then she went to stay with her sister Mary at Uppercross.

At Uppercross, Mary was lying on a sofa and complaining that nobody cared about her. Anne listened patiently, made the room comfortable, and found that she was needed there, which was a pleasant feeling.
Charles Musgrove's family lived nearby in a warm, noisy house full of music and laughter. His two sisters, Louisa and Henrietta, were pretty, cheerful girls who loved to dance and walk.
One morning Charles Musgrove told everyone that Captain Wentworth was coming to visit his sister at Kellynch Hall. Anne said nothing, but she knew that she would soon see the man she had lost.
When Captain Wentworth came into the room, he bowed politely and said a few words to Anne. His manner was correct but cold, as if she were a stranger, and she felt herself go red and then pale.
Anne soon learned that Wentworth had told his sister that she was so altered that he hardly knew her. The words hurt her deeply, although she had always known that her looks had faded.

Captain Wentworth became the favourite of the whole Musgrove family, and he talked and laughed as if he had no cares. He said that he wished to marry soon, and that he wanted a woman with a firm and strong mind.
Henrietta had loved her cousin Charles Hayter, a young clergyman, until Captain Wentworth came. Now both sisters seemed to like the Captain, and nobody knew which of them he preferred.

Little Walter, Mary's naughty younger son, climbed on Anne's back while she was kneeling beside his sick brother. Suddenly the boy was pulled away, and she saw that Captain Wentworth had done it without a word.

The young people walked to Winthrop on a bright autumn day, and Anne rested behind a hedge to catch her breath. She heard Wentworth tell Louisa that a firm mind was like a nut that hangs on, shining and sound.

Admiral and Mrs Croft saw Anne tired on the road and offered her a place in their little carriage. On the way, the Admiral talked cheerfully about how his brother-in-law might marry one of the Miss Musgroves.

Soon the young people decided to visit Lyme, a small town on the sea, where Captain Wentworth had friends. The group arrived at an inn, and Anne was charmed by the cliffs, the harbour and the cool air.
Captain Harville was a naval friend of Wentworth, and his family lived in a tiny but happy house by the water. He was lame from an old wound, and his guest, Captain Benwick, was a quiet young man.

Captain Benwick had been engaged to Captain Harville's sister Fanny, but she had died while he was at sea. He read sad poetry all day, and Anne gently suggested that he should also read some strong prose.
While Anne walked on the beach, a gentleman looked at her with clear admiration as he passed. Wentworth saw it, and for the first time he looked at her as if he had remembered who she was.
On the Cobb, the long stone wall by the sea, Louisa was determined to be jumped down the steps by Wentworth. He caught her once, but she begged to do it again, and she jumped before he was ready.
Louisa was lying on the stones, with her eyes closed and her face white, and everyone thought she was dead. Wentworth cried that he had killed her, and he looked as if he would faint himself.
Anne was the only person who did not lose her head, and she told the others quickly what to do. Wentworth called out for anyone to help him, and she saw how deeply he cared about Louisa.
The men carried Louisa gently to the Harvilles' house, where the surgeon examined her head. He said that the injury was serious, but that she was alive and that there was still hope.
After the accident, Anne went back to Uppercross, where Lady Russell came to take her away to Bath. Louisa stayed at Lyme to get better, and the Harvilles looked after her with great kindness.

Sir Walter and Elizabeth had rented a fine house in Camden Place, and they enjoyed showing it to visitors. Mrs Clay was still living with them, and Anne noticed that she smiled at Sir Walter too much.
One day Mr William Elliot came to visit, because he was Sir Walter's cousin and would inherit his title. Years before, he had insulted the family, but now he spoke kindly and wished to be friends.

Anne realised that Mr Elliot was the same gentleman who had looked at her on the beach at Lyme. He praised her warmly, and Lady Russell began to hope that he might marry Anne and make her Lady Elliot.
In Bath, Anne found out that her school friend Mrs Smith was living in a small, cheap room, ill and alone. Mrs Smith had lost her husband and her money, but she was bright and cheerful in spirit.
A letter from Uppercross brought astonishing news: Louisa had fallen in love with Captain Benwick and was going to marry him. Anne was amazed, and she thought that Captain Wentworth must now be free.
A few days later, Captain Wentworth came to Bath, and Anne saw him in a busy shop. He spoke to her kindly and politely, and for the first time in years there was warmth in his eyes.
Wentworth noticed how often Anne was with Mr Elliot, and he began to think that she might marry him. Anne saw his sadness, and she longed to tell him the truth, but could not find the way.

Mrs Smith told Anne a surprising secret about Mr Elliot, who had once been her husband's friend. When her husband had needed help, Mr Elliot had refused, and he had never cared about anyone but himself.
Mrs Smith explained that Mr Elliot wanted to be near the family to guard his place as heir. If Sir Walter married Mrs Clay and had a son, Mr Elliot would lose the title and the fine house.
The whole family went to a concert in the Octagon Room, and Captain Wentworth was there too. Anne sat near him, and she hoped to speak to him alone, but there were many people around them.
Mr Elliot bent over Anne to whisper something kind, and Wentworth saw them together. He looked pained and jealous, said a short goodbye, and left the room before the concert ended.
The next morning Anne went to the White Hart inn to visit Mrs Musgrove, who was in Bath. Captain Harville was there as well, and Captain Wentworth sat near them, writing a letter at a desk.

Captain Harville showed her a picture of his dead sister and spoke sadly about Captain Benwick, who had forgotten her so soon. He believed that women forget their loves sooner than men do, and Anne disagreed.

Anne said that women had a quiet kind of faithfulness, because they stayed at home and had little else to think of. All the privilege she claimed, she said, was to love longest when all hope had gone.
Behind them, Captain Wentworth dropped his pen, and Anne realised that he had listened to every word. He gathered his papers and left quickly, and she did not dare to hope what it meant.
A moment later, Wentworth came back to look for his gloves, and he slipped a letter onto the table in front of Anne. It was addressed to her, and he left the room again without a word.
In the letter, Wentworth wrote that his heart was half in pain and half in hope. He said that he had loved no one but her, and he asked her for an answer.

Anne rose quickly and hurried to find Wentworth, but she knew that she could not run through the streets of Bath. Soon Charles Musgrove offered to walk her home, and Wentworth joined them as they went.
They walked down a quiet path, and at last they could speak freely. Wentworth said that he had never stopped loving her, even when he was angry, and Anne told him her heart had never changed.
Anne said that she had been young and had trusted Lady Russell, and he did not blame her any longer. Both of them had suffered, and both now knew that they had been wrong to be apart.
Lady Russell admitted that she had been mistaken about Wentworth, and she welcomed him warmly. Sir Walter agreed to the wedding, and soon Mr Elliot left Bath, taking Mrs Clay with him.

Anne married Captain Wentworth, and Mrs Smith's money was recovered with his help, so that she lived in comfort again. Anne was perfectly happy, although she sometimes feared that he might be called back to the sea.
C1C2: Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall, in Somerset, had only one book he cared to read, and he opened it each morning at the page that held his own name. Vanity was the foundation of his character: he admired his handsome face, prized his rank, and measured every other person by those two standards. Nothing in that volume ever failed to soothe him, for the Elliots had been a distinguished family for generations.

Lady Elliot had died while her girls were still young, and since then the household had been ruled by her husband's vanity and her eldest daughter's pride. Elizabeth was handsome and cold, Mary had married and complained of her health, and Anne, who was nearly always overlooked, possessed more good sense than all the rest together. Only Lady Russell, a close friend of the late Lady Elliot, valued Anne as she deserved.

Year after year Sir Walter had spent more than his estate could bear, on handsome furniture, fine carriages and every comfort that a man of his rank was supposed to need. When his lawyer, Mr Shepherd, finally laid the accounts before him, he could no longer deny that he was deeply in debt. Lady Russell urged him to practise strict economy, but every sensible plan she offered seemed to him a personal insult.

It was Mr Shepherd who finally dared to suggest that Sir Walter should let Kellynch Hall and move to Bath, where a gentleman could live with dignity on a smaller income. The war with France had ended, he pointed out, and several naval officers who had grown rich in it were now searching for a country house. Sir Walter disliked the navy, which he believed spoiled a man's looks, but he agreed in the end because there seemed no other way.

A tenant was soon found in Admiral Croft, a cheerful, weather-beaten sailor who admired the house and asked very little of it. Anne, who had listened to the arrangements in silence, learned that his wife was the sister of a certain Frederick Wentworth, and the name struck her like a bell heard across a long stretch of years. No one else in the room noticed that she had turned pale, or that she needed a moment before she could speak again.

Eight years earlier, when Anne was only nineteen, she had met Frederick Wentworth, a young naval officer who was clever, brave and full of warmth. In a few summer weeks they had fallen deeply in love, and they had promised to marry, though he possessed neither fortune nor family connections. To Anne, who had never been loved so openly before, his confidence in the future seemed more than enough to live on.

Lady Russell, who loved Anne like a daughter, argued that such an engagement was imprudent, for the young man had no money and his profession was full of danger. She spoke so kindly and so firmly that Anne, who had been taught to respect her elders, finally gave way and ended it. Wentworth left the country in anger, and Anne was left to wonder for years whether prudence had been worth what it cost.

Eight years had passed, and the bright girl of nineteen had faded into a quiet woman of twenty-seven whom her own family hardly noticed. She had never loved again, though she had received one or two proposals, and she had followed the career of Captain Wentworth through the newspapers with a mixture of pride and pain. He had won both fame and a handsome fortune at sea, and she had no reason to suppose that he had kept a single kind thought of her.

On the day of the move, Sir Walter and Elizabeth set off for Bath, taking with them Mrs Clay, a friend of Elizabeth who had made herself indispensable. Anne lingered behind to say farewell to the gardens and the walks she loved, and watched the Crofts arrive to take possession. Then she travelled the three miles to Uppercross, where her younger sister Mary had declared she could not manage without her.

Anne found her sister lying on a sofa, convinced that she was seriously ill and that nobody in the house cared a straw about it. Mary complained of her husband, of her servants and of her neighbours, and she expected Anne to listen to every grievance with sympathy. Anne, who had spent her life being useful to people who forgot to thank her, settled down to the task with composure and even a measure of relief.

Charles Musgrove's family lived in the Great House close by, and they were a warm, noisy, generous tribe who welcomed Anne at every hour of the day. His sisters Louisa and Henrietta were pretty, high-spirited girls whose education had been less careful than their father's pride in them. Anne, who was fond of music, played the piano for their dances, and was content to sit in a corner and watch them enjoy themselves.

One morning, news came that Captain Wentworth had arrived at Kellynch and would shortly call upon the Musgroves, who had heard a great deal in his praise. Mary talked of nothing else, and the girls fussed over their hair, but Anne said nothing at all. She had known for some time that this meeting must come, and she had tried a hundred times to prepare for it, yet her calm gave way the moment it was real.

When Captain Wentworth entered the Musgroves' parlour, he bowed to Anne and exchanged a few words with her, in the tone of a man speaking to a slight acquaintance. His manner was perfectly correct, and that was the cruelty of it, for there was nothing in it that she could answer or resent. She sat through the rest of the visit with a smile fixed upon her face, hearing little and understanding less.

Before long, Anne learned through a careless remark that Captain Wentworth had found her so altered that he would hardly have known her. She told herself that it was only the truth, since eight years of worry had taken her bloom, and that she had no right to be wounded. Even so, the words stayed with her for days, like a small stone she could neither swallow nor spit out.

Wentworth quickly became the darling of the whole Musgrove circle, telling tales of the sea and laughing with the sisters until the rooms rang. He let it be known that he was ready to marry, and that he wanted a woman of firm and steady character, for he had learned to despise weakness. Anne, who understood only too well whom those words were aimed at, kept her eyes on her sewing and her face still.

Henrietta had long been fond of her cousin Charles Hayter, a modest young clergyman with good prospects, but the arrival of a dashing naval hero threatened to turn her head. Louisa, who was the bolder of the sisters, soon began to claim a larger share of the Captain's attention than her sister. The Musgroves wondered aloud which of the girls he preferred, and Anne, who knew him better than any of them, found that she could not tell.

Anne was kneeling on the floor beside her ill nephew when the naughty younger boy jumped on her back and clung there stubbornly, refusing to be removed. In an instant the child was lifted away, and she realised that it was Captain Wentworth who had done it, though he left the room before she could thank him. The small act of kindness shook her more than any speech could have, for it proved that he still noticed her suffering.

On a golden autumn walk to Winthrop, the party rested in a field, and Anne, sitting on the other side of a hedge, overheard Wentworth speaking to Louisa. He praised a firmness of mind that would not bend to any persuasion, and he held up a glossy hazel nut as the emblem of a strong character. Louisa laughed delightedly, and Anne understood at last the meaning of his speech, which had been meant, in part, for her.

Admiral and Mrs Croft, driving along the lane in their small carriage, found Anne tired and kindly insisted that she ride home with them. On the way, the Admiral spoke with his usual cheerfulness of the likely marriage of his brother-in-law to one of the Miss Musgroves, and Anne listened in silence. She noticed with quiet respect how affectionately the couple behaved, and could not help imagining how happy such a life might have been.

Before long, the young people proposed a journey to Lyme, a little town on the south coast where Captain Wentworth had friends he wished to visit. Anne, who had not seen the sea for years, was enchanted by the high cliffs, the busy harbour and the fresh wind that lifted the colour back into her cheeks. They took rooms at an inn and walked down to the shore, where the waves broke white against the grey stone.

Wentworth led the party to the home of his old friend Captain Harville, who had been lamed by a wound and lived in a small house crammed with warmth and hospitality. The Harvilles received them as if they were old friends, and a quiet naval officer named Captain Benwick was introduced as their guest. Anne noticed at once how much affection the sailors had for one another, and she was moved.

Captain Benwick had been engaged to Harville's sister Fanny, who had died while he was away at sea, and he carried his grief with him like a heavy cloak. He talked to Anne for a long while about poetry, quoting lines of the saddest kind, and she, with the wisdom of long sorrow, advised him to read more prose. Her gentle counsel surprised him, and he looked at her with a respect that his shy manner could not quite conceal.

On the beach one morning, a well-dressed stranger passed Anne and turned to look at her with an expression of unmistakable admiration. The sea air had restored her bloom, and her eyes shone, so that she seemed ten years younger than the pale woman of Uppercross. Captain Wentworth observed the glance, and he turned his eyes on her with a look of such startled interest that she felt it to her fingertips.

On the long stone wall of the Cobb, Louisa, delighted with her own daring, insisted on being jumped down a flight of steps into Captain Wentworth's arms. He caught her once and warned her against repeating it, but she laughed at his caution and sprang again before he was ready. Her foot slipped, and she fell to the hard stones below, where she lay without a sound.

Louisa lay among the stones with closed eyes and a pale face, and for a terrible moment everyone present believed that she was dead. Captain Wentworth knelt beside her, holding her in his arms, and cried out in a voice of utter despair that he had killed her. The party stood paralysed with horror, and Mary screamed, and the sound of the sea seemed suddenly very cruel.

While the others wept, or wrung their hands, or stood speechless, Anne alone retained her presence of mind and told everyone what must be done. Wentworth, wild with anxiety, begged for someone to help him, and she sent for a surgeon and bade Captain Benwick run to the town. In the midst of her own anguish at the sight of his devotion to Louisa, she was acting with a clarity that surprised even herself.

Captain Harville directed that Louisa be carried to his own house, where his kind wife at once put aside her duties to take charge of the invalid. The surgeon examined the wound, declared that the injury was serious but not hopeless, and warned them that her recovery would be slow. Anne, who had asked for nothing in return, discovered that Wentworth had been watching her work, and when their eyes met, there was gratitude in his.

After the accident, Anne returned to Uppercross, now a house of whispers, where Louisa was still absent and Mary was too frightened to be useful. Soon Lady Russell arrived to carry Anne away to Bath, and the sisters took leave of each other with a feeling of sadness. Louisa, meanwhile, stayed under the Harvilles' care at Lyme, where she was slowly recovering, and where Captain Benwick was being very attentive.

At Camden Place, in the best part of Bath, Sir Walter and Elizabeth had settled into a house that was handsome enough to satisfy even their vanity. They received Anne with polite indifference and asked her nothing about Lyme, Louisa, or the accident, but only whether the house was not charming. Mrs Clay was still very much a member of the family, and Anne noticed with some alarm how often she smiled at her host.

A visitor was announced who proved to be Mr William Elliot, Sir Walter's cousin and heir, who had once insulted the family by marrying beneath him and ignoring them. He now wished to make amends, and he apologised so elegantly that Sir Walter, who loved flattery, forgave him almost at once. His manners were so perfect, and his conversation so agreeable, that the whole household was charmed.

To her surprise, Anne recognised in Mr Elliot the same gentleman who had stared at her so admiringly on the beach at Lyme. He sought her company at every opportunity and praised her good sense so warmly that she could not help being flattered, and Lady Russell began to dream of a match. How satisfying it would be, she thought, to see Anne mistress of Kellynch Hall and wearing her mother's title.

Anne learned that an old school friend, Mrs Smith, was living in Bath, and she hurried to a modest lodging where the poor woman lay crippled by illness. Her husband had died and left her in debt, yet she bore her misfortune with a cheerfulness that humbled Anne, who had far less to complain of. Sir Walter was scandalised that his daughter should visit such an unfashionable place, but Anne went anyway.

A letter from Uppercross brought news that astonished everyone: Louisa, who had been expected to marry Captain Wentworth, was engaged instead to Captain Benwick. The sad officer had fallen in love with his patient during her long recovery, and she, tender and grateful, had returned his feelings. Anne read the letter twice and, scarcely daring to hope, wondered whether Captain Wentworth might be free after all.

Within a few days, Captain Wentworth arrived in Bath, and Anne met him by chance as she sheltered from a shower in a crowded shop. He greeted her more warmly than he had done since their first meeting, and she saw with a leap of her heart that his manner had grown less guarded. Yet she was walking with Mr Elliot, and as the rain stopped, Wentworth stepped out into the street with a thoughtful face.

Captain Wentworth observed how frequently Anne was in Mr Elliot's company, and from the whispers of Bath society he drew the natural conclusion that they were soon to be engaged. Anne saw the change in his manner, a stiffness that had returned as swiftly as it had gone, and she longed to correct his mistake. But there was nothing she could say without seeming to ask for his attention, and so she suffered in silence.

At last Mrs Smith spoke plainly, for she knew that Anne might soon accept a man whose true character was hidden from her. Mr Elliot, she said, had been her husband's close friend in youth, had spent his money freely, and had abandoned him as soon as he fell into trouble. He was a man without compassion or principle, she said, who would sacrifice anyone for his own advantage.

She went on to explain that Mr Elliot had made peace with the family only because he feared that Mrs Clay would marry Sir Walter and bear him a son. A male heir would take away both his title and his hope of Kellynch, and so he had resolved to stay close to the household and keep watch. Marrying Anne, who was his cousin and trusted by Sir Walter, would be the surest way to protect his inheritance.

The Elliots and Lady Russell attended a concert in the Octagon Room, a handsome hall where all the fashionable people of Bath gathered for amusement. Anne's eyes searched the crowd until they found Captain Wentworth, who stood against a wall at some distance and seemed to avoid her glance. When he came across the room at last to speak with her, her hopes rose, though the noise of the concert made any intimate conversation impossible.

Just as their talk grew warmer, Mr Elliot leaned over Anne's chair to whisper an elegant compliment, and Wentworth, watching from a distance, reddened with jealousy. He bowed to her with a coldness she could scarcely endure, murmured a brief goodbye, and left the room before the music had ended. Anne sat motionless, wondering whether she had lost for the second time the only man she had ever loved.

The next morning, Anne called at the White Hart to visit Mrs Musgrove, who had come to Bath, and found Captain Harville already there. Captain Wentworth sat at a table across the room, writing a letter and apparently absorbed in it, though Anne suspected that he heard every word that was spoken. She settled by the window with Captain Harville, hardly knowing what she would say.

Captain Harville was troubled by the speed with which Benwick had forgotten his sister Fanny, and he lamented it to Anne in a low voice. Men, he said, loved less deeply than women, and forgot more easily, though he supposed that it was only the nature of the sex. Anne, who had her own long experience of constancy to draw on, begged leave to differ, and the dispute grew more earnest.

Anne answered that women had been robbed of their voices by the men who wrote the books, and that they had the harder lot, for they stayed at home with their sorrow while men had work to occupy them. All the privilege she claimed for her own sex, she said, was that of loving longest when existence or hope was gone. She spoke in a low and trembling voice, unable to look toward the table where Wentworth sat.

Behind them came the soft clatter of a pen falling on the floor, and Anne realised that Captain Wentworth had heard everything she had said. He gathered up his papers in a flurry and hurried from the room, murmuring something about an errand, and she dared not guess what it meant. She sat shaking, not knowing whether she had spoiled everything or won something precious.

A few minutes afterward, Wentworth came back to the room, saying that he had forgotten his gloves, and walked quickly to the table where Anne sat. He placed beside her a folded paper bearing the words, in his strong handwriting, that it was for Miss Anne Elliot, and he left again before she could move. Anne could hardly breathe, because she understood that what he had been writing so long was not for Mrs Musgrove.

In the letter, Captain Wentworth confessed that she pierced his soul, that he was half agony and half hope, and that he could no longer remain silent. He had never loved any woman but her, he wrote, and had been unjust, weak and resentful, but never inconstant. If she still felt as she did eight years before, he asked her to let him know it by a single look before the evening.

Anne could not run through the streets of Bath, though every nerve urged her to find Captain Wentworth at once, and she was glad when Charles Musgrove offered to escort her. Wentworth appeared a few moments later, as if by chance, and Charles, who understood a good deal more than he showed, found a reason to leave them. At last the two were left alone on the pavement, with all the long silence of eight years between them.

They walked along a quiet gravel path, away from the crowds, and there at last they were able to speak with perfect openness. Wentworth confessed that he had been proud and angry for years, that he had tried to love others and failed, and that he had never forgotten her. Anne, in return, told him that her heart had been his from the first and that no later attachment had ever been able to replace him.

Anne said that she had been very young and had trusted a friend whom she respected, and that she did not think she had been wrong to be guided by her, though it had cost her dearly. Wentworth admitted that he had been unjust to judge her so harshly, and that her gentleness was the very quality he had needed most. Neither of them could bear to remember the lost years, and neither wished to dwell on them any longer.

Lady Russell, who had long since repented of her advice, admitted that she had misjudged Captain Wentworth and gladly welcomed him to the family. Sir Walter, whose pride was soothed by the Captain's wealth and fame, gave his consent, and Elizabeth did the same. Meanwhile Mr Elliot, finding all his plans overthrown, left Bath in haste, and it was soon whispered that Mrs Clay had gone with him.

Anne and Captain Wentworth were married, and no couple had ever waited longer or deserved their happiness more. With Wentworth's help, Mrs Smith's lost property in the West Indies was recovered, so that her old age was no longer shadowed by poverty. Anne, who had spent so many years in sadness, felt only one slight cloud in her new life, which was the fear that war might one day call her husband back to sea.
